fd_0064.says: Soft Louisiana sausage of pork, rice and liver, squeezed from its casing
fd_0064.why: That is boudin. This one is chunked pork, firm and smoked, sliced into coins.

fd_0065.says: Spicy pork sausage colored red with tomato and cayenne, always sold raw
fd_0065.why: The red comes from paprika or dried chiles, and the Spanish kind is dry-cured, not fresh.

fd_0066.says: Italian sausage of ground pork neck, fermented and dried in a casing
fd_0066.why: It is one whole muscle cured intact, not ground meat, even though it dries in a casing.

fd_0067.says: Pork leg soaked in a sweet brine, then baked and glazed until moist
fd_0067.why: That describes the wet-cured city style. This one is rubbed with dry salt and aged, never soaked in brine.

fd_0068.says: Italian pork jowl, heavily smoked like bacon, then diced into pasta
fd_0068.why: It is cured and air-dried without smoke, which is what sets it apart from bacon.

fd_0069.says: Rendered pork fat, melted and strained, used for frying and pastry
fd_0069.why: That is lard. This is a solid slab of back fat, cured and sliced, never melted down.

fd_0070.says: Cured pork tenderloin from Spain, the small soft muscle under the spine
fd_0070.why: It is the loin, the large muscle along the back. In Spain the tenderloin is called solomillo.

fd_0071.says: Italian dry-cured pork leg, diced small and crisped for pasta sauces
fd_0071.why: It is the belly, not the leg. A dry-cured pork leg is a ham, such as prosciutto.

fd_0072.says: Brined beef that is only smoked, then dried and sliced cold like a ham
fd_0072.why: Smoke is not the last step: it is steamed for hours until tender and usually served warm.

fd_0072.says: Beef rubbed with pepper and oven roasted, with no brine and no smoke
fd_0072.why: That is roast beef. The days in brine and the smoke are what make it what it is.

fd_0073.says: Smooth paste of pure liver, always made with no other meat or fat
fd_0073.why: Liver is common but not required, and most are built on pork and fat with other meats.

fd_0074.says: Italian pork leg, smoked over beechwood and cooked before slicing
fd_0074.why: The crudo style taught here is never smoked or cooked: salt, air and time do the work.

fd_0076.says: Smoked Alpine pork leg, fully cooked and carved thick like deli ham
fd_0076.why: It is never cooked: it is cured, cold smoked and aged, then sliced thin and eaten as it is.

fd_0077.says: Mild, sweet ham from the pork hind leg, carved thick as a main course
fd_0077.why: It is spicy shoulder, not leg, and it seasons a dish in small dice instead of being carved.

fd_0078.says: Any shared board of cheese, fruit, nuts and crackers, with or without meat
fd_0078.why: The word means prepared meats. A board with no cured meat is a cheese or snack board.

fd_0079.says: Lean pork loin from the Italian Alps, salt-cured and air-dried firm
fd_0079.why: It is beef, which is why it is the lean, dark red meat on a board that is mostly pork.

fd_0081.says: Calabrian chili paste made with olive oil, with no meat in it at all
fd_0081.why: It is a cured pork salami first. The chili is a seasoning, and the softness comes from pork fat.

fd_0082.says: Everyday Spanish ham from white pigs, dried in mountain air for a year
fd_0082.why: That describes serrano. This ham comes from Iberian-breed pigs and ages far longer.

fd_0082.says: Spanish ham heavily smoked over oak, then cooked and sliced thick
fd_0082.why: It is never smoked or cooked, only salted and air-dried, and it is carved very thin.

fd_0084.says: Deep lidded bowl for serving soup, and the hot soup ladled out of it
fd_0084.why: That is a tureen. This is a cold, sliced loaf named for the mold it is baked in.

fd_0085.says: Brisket slow-cooked with sweet corn kernels, an Irish American classic
fd_0085.why: Corn here is an old word for the coarse grains of salt used in the cure, not the vegetable.

fd_0086.says: Thick layer of outside fat trimmed from the top of a beef rib roast
fd_0086.why: It is a muscle, not a fat layer, and it is the most prized meat on the steak.

fd_0087.says: Lean, naturally soft muscle from the face that cooks quickly like a steak
fd_0087.why: It is tough and full of connective tissue, and only hours of braising make it soft.

fd_0089.says: The pig's foot below the ankle, all skin and small bones, pickled or stewed
fd_0089.why: That is the trotter. This is the joint just above it, where the leg meets the foot.

fd_0090.says: The strips of meat from between the bones of a rack of barbecue ribs
fd_0090.why: It is the large muscle lying on top of the rib bones, not the meat between them.

fd_0091.says: Tender, lightly worked roast above the front leg needing only a quick sear
fd_0091.why: It works hard and is tough until long, slow cooking melts its connective tissue.

fd_0092.says: Beef from the brisket, the breast muscle, sold on a small piece of bone
fd_0092.why: It comes from the lower rib cage in the chuck and plate, next to the brisket but not part of it.

fd_0093.says: The wide, lean roast along the back of a pig that chops are cut from
fd_0093.why: That is the loin. The tenderloin is the small tapered muscle tucked beneath it.

fd_0094.says: The pig's stomach lining, an organ meat simmered for hours until it turns soft
fd_0094.why: It is muscle and fat from the underside of the animal, not the stomach or any organ.

fd_0095.says: A thin, lean steak sliced from the round, the hard-working back leg
fd_0095.why: It comes from the short loin along the back, a tender area, not from the leg.

fd_0096.says: Two regional names for exactly the same steak, identical in size and makeup
fd_0096.why: They differ in how much tenderloin they carry: the porterhouse has the wider piece.

fd_0096.says: A steak pairing ribeye and tenderloin on either side of one central rib
fd_0096.why: The large side is strip loin, not ribeye, and the cut comes from the short loin, behind the ribs.

fd_0100.says: A thin steak pounded out with a mallet and seared under a heavy press
fd_0100.why: The name describes the shape of the muscle, not a way of pounding or pressing it.

fd_0101.says: A style of slow smoked barbecue, not any particular part of the animal
fd_0101.why: It is a specific cut, the chest of the steer, and it is braised and cured as well as smoked.

fd_0103.says: The upper thigh of the animal, lean and tender enough to grill as a steak
fd_0103.why: It is the lower leg, the shin, and it is far too sinewy to grill. It needs hours of braising.

fd_0104.says: A lean steak from the hind leg that has to be braised to turn tender
fd_0104.why: It comes from the sirloin, not the leg, and it is tender enough to grill or roast.

fd_0105.says: The belly ribs of a young sheep, slow-smoked like barbecue spare ribs
fd_0105.why: It is the upper ribs with the tender loin eye attached, roasted fast and served pink.

fd_0106.says: A loin slice from the hog that is only ever served well done, never pink
fd_0106.why: Since 2011 the national guidance has been 63 C (145 F) with a rest, and many kitchens serve a blush of pink.

fd_0106.says: A thick slice of the hog's hind leg, cured and smoked before it is grilled
fd_0106.why: That is a ham steak. This cut is fresh meat from the loin along the back, not cured leg.

fd_0107.says: Beef from cattle massaged daily and fed beer to make the meat tender
fd_0107.why: That is mostly legend. The marbling comes from breeding and long, careful feeding.

fd_0107.says: A protected name for beef raised only around the city of Kobe
fd_0107.why: That describes Kobe, one regional brand. The word covers the Japanese breeds wherever they are raised.
